answer:
**Short answer:** the papers find a cost only when a window is added to a model that was trained without one. Models trained with the window from the start show little or no loss: Mistral 7B claims none, and Gemma 3 measures almost none. GLM-5 retrofitted a window onto an existing model and long-context retrieval collapsed. Phi-4 dropped its predecessor's window but gives no reason.

## Mistral 7B: no loss claimed, but nothing isolates the window

- **How it works.** Every layer attends only to the previous W = 4096 tokens. Stacking layers lets information travel further: after k layers it can move k×W tokens, so the last layer has a "theoretical attention span" of about 131K tokens ([p. 2, Sliding Window Attention](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Mistral%207B.pdf?dest=section.2&page=2)). The window size is in [p. 2, Table 1](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Mistral%207B.pdf?dest=table.1&page=2).
- **What it saves.** The KV cache is a rolling buffer of size W, which uses 8x less cache memory at 32k tokens "without impacting the model quality". Kernel changes give a 2x speed-up at 16K ([p. 2](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Mistral%207B.pdf?dest=section.2&page=2&search=without%20impacting%20the%20model%20quality)).
- **Caveat.** "Without impacting the model quality" is stated, not shown. There is no ablation of the window, of grouped-query attention or of the data. The model beats Llama 2 13B on every benchmark tested ([p. 3, Table 2](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Mistral%207B.pdf?dest=table.2&page=3)), but the paper discloses nothing about its training data, so that win can't be credited to the window.

## Gemma 3: measured, almost no perplexity cost

- **Design.** Five local sliding-window layers for each global layer, with a 1024-token local window. Only the global layers see the long context ([p. 1](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Gemma%203%20Technical%20Report.pdf?dest=section.2&page=1)).
- **Ratio ablation.** Changing the local:global ratio, from Gemma 2's 1:1 up to 7:1, has "minimal impact on perplexity" ([p. 6, Fig. 3](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Gemma%203%20Technical%20Report.pdf?dest=figure.3&page=6)).
- **Window ablation.** "The sliding window can be reduced significantly without impacting perplexity" ([p. 6, Fig. 4](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Gemma%203%20Technical%20Report.pdf?dest=figure.4&page=6)).
- **Memory saving.** At 32k context, a global-only model has 60% KV-cache memory overhead. With one global layer per three local layers and a 1024 window, the overhead is under 15% ([p. 6, Fig. 5](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Gemma%203%20Technical%20Report.pdf?dest=figure.5&page=6)).
- **Caveats.**
  - The ablations use 2B text-only models.
  - The only measure is validation perplexity, not long-context retrieval.
  - The results are only in figures; the text gives no numbers.
  - The memory figure is for that 1:3 setup, not the 5:1 one Gemma 3 ships.

## Phi-4: went back to full attention, without saying why

Phi-4 uses "full attention over the 4K context length, rather than a 2K sliding window used in phi-3-medium" ([p. 7, §3](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Phi-4%20Technical%20Report.pdf?dest=section.3&page=7&search=sliding%20window)). The report gives no reason and no ablation, so this is a design choice, not evidence of a cost.

## GLM-5: retrofitting a window costs a lot on long context

GLM-5 tested this on GLM-9B, a model already trained with full attention ([§2.1.2, p. 6](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/GLM-5.%20from%20Vibe%20Coding%20to%20Agentic%20Engineering.pdf?dest=subsubsection.2.1.2&page=6)). Half the layers were converted to a 4096-token window, either by plain alternation ("SWA Interleave") or by choosing the layers with a beam search on RULER at 16K ("SWA Pattern").

**Without retraining** (RULER scores, Table 4, pp. 6–7):

| Context | Full attention | Interleave | Searched pattern |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8K | 93.67 | 54.02 | 92.54 |
| 128K | 75.28 | 6.51 | 53.95 |

**After 190B tokens of continued training at 64K** (scores at 128K, [p. 7, Table 5](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/GLM-5.%20from%20Vibe%20Coding%20to%20Agentic%20Engineering.pdf?dest=table.5&page=7)):

| Benchmark | Full attention | Interleave | Searched pattern |
|---|---|---|---|
| RULER | 75.28 | 44.93 (−30.35) | 69.59 (−5.69) |
| RepoQA | 65.83 | 39.33 (−26.50) | 51.17 (−14.66) |
| MRCR | 35.39 | 28.83 (−6.56) | 33.58 (−1.81) |

The paper calls plain alternation "catastrophic degradation" on long-context tasks. It says every efficient variant leaves a gap on fine-grained retrieval, "even when half of the layers retain full attention" (p. 7). GLM-5 itself uses DeepSeek Sparse Attention, which chooses tokens by content instead of a fixed window ([p. 5](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/GLM-5.%20from%20Vibe%20Coding%20to%20Agentic%20Engineering.pdf?dest=subsubsection.2.1.1&page=5)).

## Reading the four together

- **How the window got there matters most.** Trained with it from the start, the cost is small (Gemma 3) or not reported (Mistral). Added after full-attention training, long-context retrieval breaks, and continued training only partly repairs it (GLM-5).
- **Which layers keep full attention matters.** Choosing them well cut GLM-5's RULER@128K loss from 30 points to 6 (p. 7, Table 5).
- **The evidence is thin.** No paper ablates a trained-in window on long-context retrieval tasks. Gemma 3 only measures perplexity on small models, which may not show retrieval failures.

**Page uncertainty:** the GLM-5 paper doesn't mark which page each table is on. I put Table 5 on p. 7 based on the area review, and Table 4 somewhere in pp. 6–7. I didn't open the PDFs. The library has no open conversion issues on the passages used here.

The foundation-models review already has a short Q&A entry on this question (`reviews/llm/foundation-models.md`), so I didn't add one.
